A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Continuous Thought Machines. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original CTM and baseline experiments on image classification, mazes, parity, sorting, Q&A MNIST, and reinforcement learning.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds component-ablation experiments on smaller mazes, including numerical results in Table 5.

M1.justification: The recurrent synapse model, private neuron-level models, sampled synchronization with temporal decay, attention/output projections, and minimum-loss/maximum-certainty objective are retained. Sorting and reinforcement-learning adaptations already appear in v1. The new ablated architectures are experimental comparators, not revisions to the proposed CTM.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluation on 15 × 15 mazes for component ablations, while omitting v1's all-positive parity test case shown in Figure 21. The major task families remain covered, with CIFAR, sorting, Q&A MNIST, and reinforcement learning relocated to Appendix G.

E2.justification: Appendix G.3 adds three evaluated comparators: CTM without NLMs, CTM without synchronization, and LSTM with synchronization. Their approximately parameter-matched comparison substantially strengthens the direct investigation of the defining components beyond v1's feed-forward and conventional LSTM comparisons. Existing comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: The new maze ablation introduces a controlled protocol matching four configurations to approximately nine million parameters and training each for 100,000 iterations (Appendix G.3, Table 4). This supplements the retained experiments rather than establishing revised training budgets or settings for their original results.

E4.justification: v4 adds direct component-removal and component-transfer tests in Appendix G.3, addressing questions that v1's width and internal-tick ablations did not isolate. Appendix I also reports additional behavioral observations, including maze-solving double takes and strategies under constraints. Conversely, v1's explicit all-positive parity failure analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Figure 26 explicitly specifies standard deviations across two seeds for the new maze ablation, adding a distinct repeated-run specification. Existing three-run analyses and uncertainty reporting for parity, CIFAR-10, Q&A MNIST, and reinforcement learning remain; there is no reported increase in their run counts.

E6.justification: v4 Table 5 newly reports maze solve rates of 65.9 ± 5.7% for CTM, 35.0 ± 7.2% without NLMs, 37.5 ± 0.7% without synchronization, and 33.8 ± 3.3% for LSTM with synchronization. These are new small-maze comparisons, not improvements over v1's original maze scores. Major retained results, including ImageNet's 72.47% top-1 and 89.89% top-5 accuracy, are unchanged. Some earlier entries, including the parity failure example and ImageNet's 0.5-certainty-threshold panel, disappear.

T1.justification: v4 omits v1 Section 2.4's specific mathematical argument that self-pairing with a very small decay rate approximately recovers squared current activations; only the broader snapshot-recovery statement remains. The central synchronization definitions, loss, and recursive derivation are otherwise retained, with Appendix K becoming Appendix H.

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same core contributions: neuron-level temporal processing and synchronization as a latent representation, enabling interpretable sequential processing and adaptive computation across tasks. Both explicitly prioritize introducing the architecture over achieving state-of-the-art performance. Reorganized contribution bullets and experiment emphasis do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v4 interprets the new ablations as support for combining NLMs with synchronization, adds behavioral explanations such as maze double takes serving as bootstrapping, and explicitly acknowledges limited comparison depth. It also removes the all-positive parity limitation and abbreviates v1's discussion of failed snapshot representations, memory, and plasticity.

D1.justification: v4 adds ablation configuration details in Table 4 and identifies CleanRL as the PPO implementation basis. It removes detailed RL environment/reward descriptions and ImageNet's short-side-256 validation resize disclosure. Code/data wording also changes from an explicit release/checkpoint announcement to supplementary-code and publication-contingent statements, although a repository link remains. These changes concern documentation rather than demonstrated changes to existing runs.

R1.justification: The rewritten related work substantially develops the paper's positioning around synchronization. It adds explicit comparisons with Reichert and Serre and Lee et al., distinguishing learned latent synchrony from emergent or control-oriented synchrony, and expands discussion of recurrent visual attention, liquid state machines, and spiking networks. Several broader motivation and future-work references are removed.

P1.justification: v4 extensively condenses and rewrites the introduction, method, experimental narrative, and conclusion. Related work moves near the beginning; mazes, ImageNet, and parity become the main experimental narrative; other experiments move into Appendix G. Pseudocode is collected in Appendix B, and a new emergent-phenomena appendix replaces some dispersed discussion.

P2.justification: Figures are extensively recomposed, merged, and relocated: maze demonstrations lead the paper, ImageNet panels are redistributed, and parity results form a consolidated main-text figure. New ablation Figure 26 and Tables 4–5 are added, while selected older panels disappear. Labels also change; Figure 22b introduces '1 - normalized entropy' despite the accompanying text retaining normalized entropy.

improvement.justification: The parameter-matched component ablation addresses v1's lack of direct tests isolating its defining components, and the expanded synchronization-related work clarifies novelty. These gains strengthen the paper, but validation remains limited to smaller mazes and two seeds. Removing the explicit parity failure case and some reproducibility details weakens transparency, making the net improvement modest.
